skill.name: k8s-security-policies
skill.description: Build Kubernetes security policy guidance for NetworkPolicy, Pod Security Standards, RBAC, admission control, and service mesh access controls.
skill.summary: Create practical Kubernetes policy patterns for workload isolation, least-privilege access, and production hardening.
skill.author: wshobson

security_audit.summary: Static analysis reported network and command-execution patterns, but most hits are markdown formatting or defensive Kubernetes examples. One broad egress template and two RBAC examples remain security-relevant because users could copy permissive policies into production. No prompt injection or malicious execution path was found.

remediation.suggestion: Replace 0.0.0.0/0 with narrower CIDR ranges, an egress gateway, or CNI-supported domain policies where possible.

remediation.issue: Wildcard RBAC examples presented as common patterns
remediation.suggestion: Move wildcard resources and verbs into an anti-pattern section, or replace them with explicit resources and verbs.
Use a namespaced Role with resourceNames and get-only access for specific secrets. Remove list and watch on secrets.

content.value_statement: Kubernetes clusters need clear isolation, RBAC, and pod standards to reduce deployment risk. This skill provides policy patterns, templates, and review prompts for practical hardening.
actual_capabilities: Creates NetworkPolicy patterns for default deny, DNS, ingress, monitoring, HTTPS egress, database access, and namespace boundaries.
Applies Pod Security Standards labels for privileged, baseline, and restricted namespace modes.
Drafts RBAC roles, bindings, and service account guidance for common Kubernetes workloads.
Provides OPA Gatekeeper examples for required labels and admission control.
Outlines Istio mTLS and AuthorizationPolicy patterns for service-to-service access.
Suggests kubectl checks for NetworkPolicy and RBAC troubleshooting.
limitations: It does not inspect or modify a live cluster by itself.
Examples must be adapted to each CNI, namespace model, workload label set, and compliance requirement.
PodSecurityPolicy is deprecated in modern Kubernetes, so Pod Security Standards should be preferred.
Broad egress and RBAC examples need review before production use.

use_cases.title: Harden a Production Namespace
use_cases.description: Create baseline pod security, default deny networking, allowed service paths, and namespace-scoped RBAC for a workload.

use_cases.title: Review Cluster Access Controls
use_cases.description: Check RBAC examples for least privilege, service account boundaries, wildcard permissions, and secret access risks.

use_cases.title: Prepare Application Deployment Guardrails
use_cases.description: Generate practical policy requirements that application teams can follow before releasing services to Kubernetes.

prompt_templates.title: Create Starter Policies
prompt_templates.prompt: Create Kubernetes security policy guidance for a namespace named <namespace>. Include pod security labels, default deny networking, and basic RBAC.

prompt_templates.title: Review Existing Manifests
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these Kubernetes manifests for policy gaps. Focus on pod security, RBAC scope, and NetworkPolicy coverage. Explain each recommended change.

prompt_templates.title: Design Multi-Tenant Controls
prompt_templates.prompt: Design security policies for multiple teams sharing one cluster. Include namespace boundaries, service accounts, ingress rules, egress rules, and audit checks.

prompt_templates.title: Build Compliance Hardening Plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a production hardening plan for a regulated Kubernetes platform. Map controls to Pod Security Standards, RBAC, admission control, network isolation, and operations checks.

output_examples.input: Harden a production namespace for a payments service.
output: Recommended restricted pod security enforcement for the namespace.
Added default deny networking with explicit DNS and service-to-service allowances.
Flagged broad outbound access for review before deployment.

output_examples.input: Review RBAC for a backend service account.
output: Identified permissions that should be namespace scoped.
Recommended replacing wildcard access with named resources and minimal verbs.
Suggested disabling automatic token mounting unless the workload needs API access.

output_examples.input: Plan admission controls for required workload labels.
output: Outlined an OPA Gatekeeper policy for required ownership and environment labels.
Explained how to roll out audit mode before enforcement.
Included validation steps for application teams.

best_practices: Start with namespace-level Pod Security Standards and default deny NetworkPolicy rules.
Grant each workload a dedicated service account with explicit resources and minimal verbs.
Review all examples against the live CNI, ingress design, and compliance scope before applying them.
anti_patterns: Do not copy wildcard RBAC permissions into production without a documented exception.
Do not allow broad outbound egress when a narrower destination model is available.
Do not rely on policy templates without matching labels, namespaces, and service accounts.

faq.question: Does this skill apply changes automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides policy guidance and examples that a user must review before applying.

faq.question: Which Kubernetes controls does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers NetworkPolicy, Pod Security Standards, RBAC, admission control, and basic service mesh authorization patterns.

faq.question: Can it replace a cluster security audit?
faq.answer: No. It helps draft and review policies, but a live cluster audit needs real configuration and runtime data.

faq.question: Does it support modern pod security?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes Pod Security Standards examples and should prefer them over deprecated PodSecurityPolicy guidance.

faq.question: How should NetworkPolicy examples be used?
faq.answer: Use them as starting points, then adapt selectors, namespaces, ports, and egress destinations to the application.

faq.question: Is it suitable for regulated environments?
faq.answer: It can support regulated environments, but every policy should be reviewed against the required control framework.
